questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Tsinghua University is widely regarded as the leading university in China. My choice was driven by a combination of strong academic opportunities, exposure to a top-tier institution, future career prospects, and the opportunity to explore a new cultural environment.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Whether in terms of culture, academic environment, personal discovery, encounters, or landscapes, China is truly surprising and fascinating. The career opportunities are remarkable: during the exchange, I had the chance to meet and interact with high-level professionals, including executives from multinational companies, experts from the Club of Rome, professors from top universities (Harvard, MIT, Stanford), and professionals from international institutions such as the World Bank, AIIB, and the United Nations.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Beijing is generally well adapted to international students. Although most people do not speak English, it is still easy to navigate the city. Upon arrival at the airport, information is widely available in English, notably for public transportation like the subway. Regarding administrative procedures, I strongly recommend contacting and meeting your international coordinator as early as possible, as they provide essential guidance for all required steps. Starting early ensures that everything runs smoothly.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I arrived one week early to ensure that all administrative matters were in order, although most students arrive one or two days before the start of classes. Upon arrival, students are required to complete an online registration process and then report in person to Zijing Building 23, where on-site assistance is provided for administrative and enrollment procedures.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: A large amount of information is provided upon arrival, which can feel overwhelming at first. I strongly recommend writing a clear to-do list to help organize the different steps. Key tasks include completing the mandatory health check at the international hospital (it is generally easier to complete it in China, as requirements are very strict), registering online with the university, and completing the dormitory registration, among others.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: On-campus housing options are limited, but you are guaranteed a room. Initially, students can choose between a single room (no roommate) or a double room (sharing with a roommate), but in practice only double rooms are available, which works well. Accommodation is spread across three buildings: Zijing 21, 22, and 23. Zijing 23 is older but allows cooking (though cooking is generally not necessary on campus). Zijing 22 has better common areas, while Zijing 21 is more modern and conveniently close to the local canteen. I stayed in Zijing 21 and would recommend it.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Few students cook in China, as food is inexpensive. Most eat at the campus canteens, of which there are 16 across the campus. A typical meal costs around 12 yuan (1–2€). There is a wide variety of dishes, often spicy and very different from European cuisine, but it is usually easy to find options that suit your taste. Cooking facilities are available in some dorms, but most students rarely use them.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The best option is to stay in on-campus housing, as the university provides it at a very low cost (around 150€/month). Just make sure to complete the necessary procedures on time. Living off-campus is possible, but rent in Beijing is quite high (comparable to Copenhagen). When selecting a dorm room online, only double rooms are available, so indicate your preferences clearly (early riser, study habits, etc.) to help match with a compatible roommate. It is possible to change roommates later, but this involves additional administrative steps. Ideally, try to see who will already be in the room to check if the profile matches your lifestyle.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is enough housing for all students on campus. The facilities in Zijing 21 are very comfortable and modern, especially considering the low price you pay.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The university registration process generally runs smoothly if you follow the steps. However, the course registration process can be somewhat chaotic (like in every exchange I guess). While there are enough courses taught in English for all students, you may not get exactly the courses you hope for depending on your field of study. For example, I focus on climate change and its solutions. Most courses in the School of Environment were highly technical and not fully aligned with my interests, so I took courses at the School of Public Policy and Management in the field of sustainable development, which worked out very well.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process at Tsinghua University for international exchange students involves several phases. Upon arrival, students must bring their admission letter and required documents to No. 23 Zijing Building (International Student and Scholar Centre) to complete on-site registration and collect their student ID card. Course selection is divided into different periods: first for courses in the host department, then for courses in other departments, and finally an online application for special reasons. Course slots are limited and assigned on a first-come, first-served basis, so it is important to act quickly. There are also three phases for dropping or withdrawing from courses, each with strict deadlines. Exchange students can normally take up to 20 credits per semester, with a maximum of 8 credits from other departments. However, this limit can be increased to 15 credits by requesting approval from the international coordinator, which is important if there are not enough courses (and thus credits) available in your own department or school. Keep in mind that 1 Chinese credit equals 2 ECTS credits, so 15 Chinese credits are needed to fulfill the 30 ECTS requirement for a semester.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: In this regard, the international coordinator was extremely helpful. Always attentive and supportive, Ms. (NAME REDACTED) (for the 2025–2026 academic year) strives to find solutions to any issues. Don’t hesitate to contact her if you have any doubts or questions, as she can provide guidance on administrative procedures, course registration, and other practical matters.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was able to register for almost all the classes I was interested in. The system operates on a first-come, first-served basis. You select courses in your own department first, and then you can access courses from other departments. This means that if there are not enough courses in your department, you may need to take courses elsewhere. Overall, you should be able to secure most of the courses you want.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I strongly recommend contacting the professors of the courses you are interested in. You can find this information in Tsinghua’s course listing (excel) and then search online to find the professor’s contact details or office. Explain your situation to them, some professors may open additional spots if they see that you are motivated. Since course selection occurs in multiple phases, patience is key. It is normal not to have all your courses finalized in the first week. Attend as many classes as possible during the first week to explore your options and decide which courses truly interest you. In the final phase, there is a special online application allowing professors to accept students into their courses, which is why contacting them early makes the process easier.

A more practical tip: being in China is an incredible opportunity to explore the country and travel. Don’t overload yourself with difficult courses that have heavy workloads. Check the curriculum in advance and try to choose courses that are relevant to your field while also leaving time for sports, student organizations, and weekend trips to discover this wonderful country.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The professors at Tsinghua are among the best in the world. Considering that China has a population of 1.4 billion and that Tsinghua is the top university in the country, you are surrounded by the Chinese elite, both students and faculty. Many professors hold degrees from prestigious universities such as Harvard and Yale, publish research in leading academic journals like Nature, lead global research organizations, and regularly collaborate with governments and companies worldwide. Attending courses here is like taking regular classes, but with professors who have an extraordinary global network, which can be extremely valuable for your future career.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Overall, the courses in China are of a reasonable level of difficulty, assuming a normal academic background. As a French student, I found that bachelor-level courses in France are heavier, while the master’s program in Denmark tends to be somewhat lighter. Of course, this depends on your field of study. In political science, environmental studies, and economics, most grades were based on assignments or projects, making it easier to pass if you stay consistent. According to my classmates at Tsinghua, courses in mathematics, physics, and computer science can be more demanding. However, with steady effort, there is no reason to worry. If you are considering an exchange abroad, it means you are ambitious and capable of succeeding.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The University of Copenhagen and other Scandinavian universities are fantastic, with a teaching style often based on projects and strong student–professor interaction within a flat hierarchy. At Tsinghua, the approach is more traditional: professors mainly lecture while students listen and ask questions. However, several of my courses included projects that offered a great deal of freedom, similar to the Danish style, which I found very valuable and enjoyable.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. Financial Institutions and Markets (2 credits)
2. Sustainable Development (3 credits)
3. International Organisations and Global Governance (3 credits)
4. Environmental Field Trip (1 credits)
5. China Studies: Industry Society and Culture (3 Credits)
6. Research Design and Thesis Writing (3 credits)

NB: 1 chinese credit = 2 ECTS

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Financial Institutions and Markets, which provides a comprehensive overview of the finance world and was very informative. China Studies is a good backup if you need credits, offering insights into Chinese ways of thinking and including a multi-day field trip to Shandong province, which was an incredible experience. The Sustainable Development course was also excellent, with a highly knowledgeable professor and guest speakers from organizations such as the Club of Rome and the World Bank.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: China is generally very inexpensive compared to Denmark. Most of my additional expenses came from train travel outside of Beijing on weekends, as I took the opportunity to explore different regions of the country.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food on campus is very inexpensive. At the canteens, you can have a complete meal for around 1–2€, which is much cheaper than I expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As an avid traveler, I focused mainly on exploring China, but I also made many friends from around the world with whom I regularly played sports such as tennis, badminton, and table tennis. The number of clubs at Tsinghua is impressive and extremely diverse, there are over 200, covering almost anything you can imagine. I’m confident that you will find something you enjoy, whether it’s robotics, business, video game, art, or any kind of sport.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Literally anything you can imagine is available, and every student can find something that interests them. There are clubs and activities for all kinds of passions like marathons on the Great Wall of China, cooking classes, tea or wine appreciation clubs, robotics competitions, coding groups, sports teams, galas, and much more. The variety is incredible, and the opportunities to meet fellow students from around the world through these activities are endless.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: “No sport, no Tsinghua” is the university’s motto. I highly recommend participating in sports, as it is one of the best ways to meet people and unwind. Traveling is also essential. There is so much to discover in China, and it’s up to you to explore and make the most of this incredible world we live in.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There are many great cities close to Beijing that are worth visiting on weekends, such as Tianjin, Chengde, Datong, and Qingdao, all easily reachable by train. For slightly longer trips, cities like Chengdu, Xi’an, Chongqing, and Harbin offer very different experiences. Harbin is especially worth visiting during the Ice and Snow Festival in winter. China’s National Day “Golden Week” holiday runs roughly from October 1 to October 7, which is one of the busiest travel periods of the year and a fantastic time to explore the country, though you should expect crowds and book transport early. This holiday period is ideal for discovering iconic landscapes such as Inner Mongolia in the north or the dramatic karst scenery of Guilin and Zhangjiajie (the “Avatar mountains”), and it’s a unique opportunity to see how diverse China is. Even outside official holidays, China has so much to offer that it’s worth using weekends and longer breaks to make the most of your time here.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to a new culture is never completely easy, but that is also what makes the experience exciting and rewarding. Life on campus is very comfortable, with many services available to support students, which makes adapting to the local culture much smoother.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: All international students are looking to make friends, so it is easy to connect with them, especially through sports or clubs. As for Chinese students, most are curious and happy to engage in conversation. Ask them where they are from, whether they have traveled, or what their hobbies are. Making friends starts with showing genuine interest in the other person, and often these simple conversations can lead to the most meaningful and lasting friendships.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Food. Chinese cuisine is often very different from what we used to, quite spicy, oily, and fried. However, there are plenty of alternatives, including vegetarian options, in the campus canteens. With over 16 canteens offering more than 1,000 dishes, the variety is truly extraordinary and makes it easy to find meals that suit your taste.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I greatly appreciated the long-term vision that is prevalent in Chinese culture. China builds with a century-long perspective, particularly in areas like energy and urban planning. Regarding climate change, although it is the world’s largest emitter (partly due to global trade) it is actively working to decarbonize and is exemplary in deploying new energy technologies and innovations.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
One of the biggest adjustments is China’s internet ecosystem. Most Western apps are blocked, so it is essential to plan ahead and use a reliable VPN like LetsVPN (since NordVPN is not working) to stay in touch with family and friends via WhatsApp. It takes some time to get used to the local system, but it becomes manageable quickly.

Make sure to download the following apps in advance: 
- WeChat (messaging and payments), 
- Alipay (metro and payments), 
- Amap (chinese google maps), 
- Meituan (food delivery and free campus bikes), 
- 12306 (China Railway),
- Bank of China (banking).

On finance, everything is digital, and most payments are done via QR codes with WeChat and Alipay. I recommend having a local Chinese bank account to avoid international fees (like Bank of China, on campus at the C building). For example, you can withdraw money with an online bank card like Revolut at the Bank of China ATM, then deposit it back into your Chinese account, this avoids unnecessary fees.

On a practical note, since most apps rely heavily on internet and run constantly in the background, having a solid phone and a good power bank is essential for daily use.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would advise starting the visa and other administrative procedures as early as possible, as they can take some time to process. Don’t hesitate to ask questions and gather information in advance to ensure a smooth start to your exchange.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friendships I made and the unforgettable experiences I shared. I had the chance to travel to breathtaking landscapes, share countless laughs, and create memories that will stay with me forever. I am deeply grateful to all the people I met, as they made this experience truly unforgettable.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The biggest challenge for me was the language barrier. I speak English well and am used to communicating easily. It was the first time I truly felt the difference compared to my bilingual friends in Chinese. Language is not strictly necessary, you can get by with effort and technology. Nevertheless, learning even a few simple words can bring a smile to the Chinese people you meet and make interactions much more enjoyable ;)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Have a lovely day!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
